findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. It answers "what is it" and "why does it matter" before anything else on the page.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The page is Athena's home page, but its title and most of its content are about a different project, firstmate. The lede does explain this framing. Still, a newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets one paragraph about it and then a long, detailed state-machine study of another tool.
findings.source: Header: "This page is that study of firstmate." and title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: Next steps are clear and concrete. A link at the top jumps to them, and they list prerequisites, the clone command, `./setup.sh` and a sample command, `athena ask "add a changelog"`, with a note on what it does (it asks before it runs).
findings.source: Header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section

findings.text: This link sits in the header, right where a newcomer looks first, but it is meant for the project's owner, not a visitor. It is confusing there, because it is unclear whose decisions it means.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The transition cards are dense with jargon and packed qualifications. A newcomer would have to keep checking the glossary, so this section mainly serves readers who already care about how firstmate works inside.
findings.source: Transitions section, e.g. t8: "A ship or scout keeps its recorded harness and needs a note; a secondmate re-reads its pin and needs none, and a secondmate with no endpoint is recovered by the spawn script instead."

findings.text: The "Start here" section is well-scaffolded. It defines its terms before using them and walks through one task in numbered steps. That gives a newcomer a readable summary before the detailed cards.
findings.source: Start here: "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails or has no limit."

findings.text: The page is candid about gaps in its sources. This shows the traceability that Athena advertises. A newcomer may still find it odd that a term is defined by saying it is undefined.
findings.source: Words used first: "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: This section and the footer describe how the page was generated, which is internal detail. A newcomer gets nothing from it.
findings.source: About this page: "is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."

findings.text: The prerequisites are listed, but the page does not say whether running Athena needs an AI account or paid model access. A newcomer would want to know that, since the page says Athena "records what each step cost".
findings.source: Next steps: "have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code)"
